turns.speaker: p2
turns.text: Microservices are clearly the correct default in 2026. Ship them.

turns.speaker: p1
turns.text: For a three-person team, who exactly wakes up at 3am when the payment service dies?

turns.speaker: p2
turns.text: Whoever owns the service, which is the entire point of the boundary. You get independent deploys, independent scaling, independent failure domains, and a codebase where nobody has to read anyone else's ORM models to change a button. That isolation is worth real operational cost even at a small headcount, because the cost of a tangled monolith compounds every single sprint you keep adding to it.

turns.speaker: p1
turns.text: I agree, but that only holds once you have more teams than services.

turns.speaker: p2
turns.text: Well, it depends on the domain, and I am not sure that always holds for every stack.

turns.speaker: p1
turns.text: Our migration cut deploy time from 38 minutes to 4 minutes, and cold-start regressions dropped across 2000 requests per second in production.

turns.speaker: p2
turns.text: Actually, I was wrong to call it a default. It is a scaling response, not a starting point.

turns.speaker: p1
turns.text: Then we are arguing about timing, not architecture.

turns.speaker: p2
turns.text: Timing is architecture. If you wait until the monolith hurts, you are refactoring under load, with production traffic on top of you and a team that has already built six months of cross-cutting assumptions into every module boundary you now need to cut. Extraction is dramatically cheaper before the coupling calcifies, and every team that waited says the same thing afterwards.

turns.speaker: p1
turns.text:
Then explain this deploy config:
```yaml
services: 11
engineers: 3
oncall_rotation: 1
```
That is not a boundary, that is a pager assigned to one person.

turns.speaker: p2
turns.text: Timing really is architecture. If you wait until the monolith hurts you end up refactoring under load, with production traffic on top of you and a team that already built months of cross-cutting assumptions into every boundary you now have to cut.

turns.speaker: p1
turns.text: Anyway, the real constraint is hiring, not topology. Nobody joins a startup to maintain a service mesh.

turns.speaker: p2
turns.text: Is a shared database not the exact coupling you claim to be avoiding?

turns.speaker: p1
turns.text: You are right. I concede that one.

turns.speaker: p2
turns.text: Then the disagreement narrows to team size, and team size changes faster than architecture does. Plan for the team you are hiring toward, not the one you have this quarter.

turns.speaker: p1
turns.text: Planning for a team you do not have is how you get 11 services and 3 engineers. Our incident count went up 4x in the first month after the split, and mean time to recovery went from 12 minutes to 51 minutes.

turns.speaker: p2
turns.text: Incident count going up is a monitoring artifact, not a reliability signal. You did not have per-service alerting before, so every failure that used to be an unnoticed 500 in one big log stream is now a named page against a named owner. That is the system working as designed, and treating raw alert volume as a regression is exactly the mistake teams make when they measure the new architecture with the old dashboard.

turns.speaker: p1
turns.text: I agree, but a page a human ignores is not observability, it is noise with a name.

turns.speaker: p2
turns.text: Noise you can route beats silence you cannot.

turns.speaker: p1
turns.text: Then route this: we merged two services back together last quarter and p99 latency fell 31%, on-call pages fell from 22 per week to 5, and nobody has asked to split them again.
